producer_brief.topic_summary: V7.0 Autonomous Ultra Monarch Remaster of Specimen BP/1/5558 (~250 Ma Early Triassic Karoo Basin, Fernandez et al., PLOS ONE 2013): active desert trench brush excavation physically splits open a red sandstone burrow cast to reveal a curled mammal-relative (Thrinaxodon) beside a wounded amphibian (Broomistega).
producer_brief.core_dramatic_question: Why were a carnivorous mammal-relative and a water-loving amphibian fossilized peacefully nose-to-tail inside one sun-baked South African desert rock?
producer_brief.target_emotion_arc: Tactile ASMR brush-dig hook -> awe as the sandstone cap cracks open in golden sun-shafts -> neurological jolt at -240 dBFS 'Wait. They were not enemies.' -> deep empathy as the limping, breathing amphibian finds refuge beside sleepy blinking Thrinaxodon -> monumental HUD-free monsoon burial.
producer_brief.audience_takeaway: Three consecutive healing rib calluses (#4-#6) and zero tooth punctures prove the injured amphibian limped into an aestivating Thrinaxodon's cool burrow to survive lethal Early Triassic heat before a monsoon flash flood sealed them together for 250 million years.

observed_evidence: Synchrotron micro-CT of Karoo Basin burrow cast BP/1/5558 revealed articulated skeletons of Thrinaxodon liorhinus and Broomistega putterilli in direct contact.
Broomistega preserves consecutive fractured right ribs (#4-#6) with bony healing calluses and zero predator bite marks on skull or postcrania.
scientific_inferences: Thrinaxodon was aestivating (dormant drought torpor) inside its cool underground chamber when the injured amphibian crawled in for shelter.
A sudden overbank monsoon flash flood rapidly filled the burrow with fine terracotta silt and preserved both animals undisturbed.
illustrative_abstractions: Physical cleavage lift of the upper sandstone nodule cap with volumetric golden dust shafts, brief warm anatomical life-silhouettes in S03, and #E63926 vermilion pathology focus on healing rib calluses.
